lessons.title: Cell structure
lessons.summary: Compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, learn the job of each subcellular structure, see how cells become specialised, and use microscopes and the magnification equation.
objectives: I can describe the differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.
I can state the function of each subcellular structure in animal, plant and bacterial cells.
I can explain how specialised cells are adapted to their function.
I can compare light and electron microscopes and use magnification = image size ÷ real size.
I can describe how microorganisms are grown safely using aseptic technique.

activities.title: Two kinds of cell
activities.content:
## Eukaryotes and prokaryotes

Every living thing is built from cells, but not all cells are built the same way.

**Eukaryotic cells** (animal, plant and fungal cells) are relatively large and have a **nucleus** that holds the genetic material inside a membrane. They also contain other membrane-bound structures such as mitochondria.

**Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria) are much smaller, typically about a tenth of the size of a eukaryotic cell. They have **no nucleus**. Instead, a single circular loop of DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm, and there may be one or more small extra rings of DNA called **plasmids**.

| Feature | Eukaryotic | Prokaryotic |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | Yes | No (DNA loop in cytoplasm) |
| Plasmids | No | Often |
| Mitochondria | Yes | No |
| Typical size | 10–100 µm | 0.2–2 µm |

A handy memory hook: pro-karyote means *before the nucleus*, and bacteria evolved before cells with a nucleus existed.

activities.title: Worked example: sorting cells
activities.content:
**A scientist looks at two cells. Cell A is 50 µm across and has a nucleus. Cell B is 1 µm across, has no nucleus and contains a plasmid. Which is which?**

- Cell A: large, has a nucleus → **eukaryotic** (could be an animal or plant cell).
- Cell B: tiny, no nucleus, has a plasmid → **prokaryotic** (a bacterium).

Two clues are enough. The presence or absence of a nucleus is the most reliable test; size and plasmids back it up.

Remember that the *unit* µm (micrometre) is one thousandth of a millimetre, so 1 µm = 0.001 mm. A bacterium at 1 µm is far too small to see with the naked eye.

question.text: Which of the following statements about prokaryotic cells are correct? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about where the DNA is kept in a bacterium.
question.explanation: Bacteria have no nucleus; their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, often with plasmids. They are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and have no mitochondria.

options.text: They are usually larger than animal cells.
options.feedback: Bacteria are far smaller than animal cells.
Mitochondria are only found in eukaryotic cells.

activities.title: Inside an animal cell
activities.content:
## Subcellular structures in animal cells

Each part of a cell has a job. You need to know these five for animal cells:

- **Nucleus** – contains the genetic material (DNA) and controls the activities of the cell.
- **Cytoplasm** – a jelly-like liquid where most chemical reactions happen. It contains enzymes that speed those reactions up.
- **Cell membrane** – a thin, flexible layer that controls which substances move into and out of the cell.
- **Mitochondria** – the site of **aerobic respiration**, which releases energy the cell can use. Busy cells have lots of them.
- **Ribosomes** – tiny structures where **proteins are made** (protein synthesis).

### Plant cells have three extras

- **Cell wall** – made of **cellulose**, it gives the cell strength and a fixed shape.
- **Permanent vacuole** – filled with **cell sap**, it keeps the cell firm and stores dissolved sugars and salts.
- **Chloroplasts** – contain **chlorophyll** and are where **photosynthesis** takes place.

Bacterial cells share the cytoplasm, membrane and ribosomes, and also have a cell wall (but it is *not* made of cellulose).

activities.title: Worked example: linking structure to job
activities.content:
**A student is asked: "Which structure would you expect to find in large numbers in a cell that makes lots of protein, and why?"**

Step 1 – identify the process: making protein = protein synthesis.

Step 2 – match the process to the structure: protein synthesis happens at **ribosomes**.

Step 3 – explain the link: more ribosomes means more protein can be made at once.

**Model answer:** *Ribosomes, because they are the site of protein synthesis, so having many of them lets the cell produce protein quickly.*

Use this three-step approach for any "structure and function" question: name the process, name the structure, then join them with **because**.

question.text: Match each subcellular structure to its function.
question.hint: Think about which structure is involved in energy release, protein making, control and photosynthesis.
question.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration; ribosomes make proteins; the nucleus controls the cell; chloroplasts are where photosynthesis takes place.

pairs.right: Contains DNA and controls the cell

activities.title: Specialised cells
activities.content:
## Specialised cells

As an organism develops, most cells **differentiate**: they gain features that suit one particular job. In animals this mostly happens early in life; many plant cells keep the ability to differentiate throughout the plant's life.

| Cell | Adaptation | Why it helps |
|---|---|---|
| Sperm cell | Long tail, many mitochondria, enzymes in the head | Swims to the egg, has energy to do so, digests its way in |
| Nerve cell | Very long, branched ends | Carries electrical signals over long distances and connects to other cells |
| Muscle cell | Contains protein filaments, many mitochondria | Can contract and has plenty of energy to do it |
| Root hair cell | Long extension, no chloroplasts | Large surface area to absorb water and minerals from soil |
| Xylem cell | Hollow tube, walls strengthened with lignin, no end walls | Carries water up the plant and supports the stem |
| Phloem cell | Sieve plates at ends, few subcellular structures | Lets dissolved sugars flow through from cell to cell |

In every case the question to ask is: *what does this cell have to do, and which feature makes that easier?*

question.text: Root hair cells have a long, thin extension sticking out into the soil. Explain how this adaptation helps the cell carry out its function.
question.hint: What does the root hair cell need to take in, and what does a bigger surface allow?
question.explanation: The extension increases the surface area of the cell, so more water and mineral ions can be absorbed from the soil at the same time.

markScheme.criterion: States that the extension increases the surface area
Links this to absorbing more water and/or mineral ions

activities.title: Microscopes and magnification
activities.content:
## Seeing cells

Cells are too small to see unaided, so we use microscopes. Two properties matter:

- **Magnification** – how many times larger the image is than the real object.
- **Resolution** – how close together two points can be and still be seen as separate. Higher resolution means a sharper, more detailed image.

**Light microscopes** shine light through a thin specimen. They are cheap, portable and can view living cells, but their magnification (up to about ×2000) and resolution are limited. You can see the nucleus and cell wall, but not ribosomes.

**Electron microscopes** use a beam of electrons instead of light. Electrons have a much shorter wavelength, so these microscopes give **far higher magnification and resolution** – enough to see mitochondria, ribosomes and the internal structure of chloroplasts. They are expensive, very large and the specimen must be dead and in a vacuum.

### The magnification equation

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{size of image}}{\text{size of real object}}$$

Both sizes must be in the **same unit** before you divide. Magnification has no unit; write it as ×400, for example.

activities.title: Worked example: using the equation
activities.content:
**An image of a cell measures 30 mm across. The real cell is 0.05 mm wide. What is the magnification?**

Both values are already in mm, so:

magnification = 30 ÷ 0.05 = **×600**

**A different cell is viewed at ×400 and the image is 20 mm wide. What is the real width in micrometres?**

1. Rearrange: real size = image size ÷ magnification = 20 ÷ 400 = 0.05 mm
2. Convert to µm: 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.05 mm = **50 µm**

The magnification triangle works just like speed = distance ÷ time: **image** goes on top, with **magnification** and **real size** underneath.

Always check units. A common slip is dividing millimetres by micrometres without converting, which gives an answer 1000 times too small.

question.text: A plant cell is viewed under a microscope. The image is 40 mm wide and the real cell is 80 µm wide. Calculate the magnification.
question.hint: Convert 80 µm into mm first (divide by 1000), then divide image size by real size.

activities.title: Growing microorganisms safely
activities.content:
## Culturing microorganisms

Bacteria divide by **binary fission**, splitting in two as often as every 20 minutes when conditions are warm and there is plenty of food. That rapid growth lets us study them in the lab, but only if we keep our cultures pure and ourselves safe.

Bacteria are grown in a **nutrient broth** or on **agar gel** in a Petri dish. To avoid contamination we use **aseptic technique**:

1. **Sterilise** Petri dishes and agar before use (usually by heating).
2. Pass the **inoculating loop** through a Bunsen flame before and after transferring bacteria.
3. Lift the lid only slightly and work close to the flame so airborne microbes are drawn upwards, away from the dish.
4. **Tape** the lid on (but not all the way round, so oxygen can still enter and dangerous anaerobic bacteria cannot thrive).
5. Store the dish **upside down** so condensation does not drip onto the colonies.
6. In school, incubate at **25 °C**, never body temperature, to reduce the chance of growing pathogens that infect humans.

If a bacterium divides every 30 minutes, after 3 hours (6 divisions) one cell becomes $2^6 = 64$ cells.

question.text:
A student wants to grow bacteria on an agar plate to test how well a new disinfectant works.

(a) Describe **two** aseptic techniques the student should use and explain why each one is needed.

(b) The student incubates the plate at 25 °C rather than 37 °C. Explain why.
question.hint: Think about how to stop unwanted microbes getting in, and about which temperature suits microbes that can infect people.
question.explanation: (a) Flaming the inoculating loop kills bacteria on it so only the chosen bacteria are transferred; sterilising the agar and dish kills any microbes already present; taping the lid stops airborne microbes entering. (b) 37 °C is human body temperature, so bacteria that grow well at it are more likely to be harmful to humans; 25 °C limits the growth of such pathogens while still allowing the culture to grow.

markScheme.criterion: Names one aseptic technique (e.g. flame the loop, sterilise agar/dish, tape the lid, work near a flame)
Explains the technique prevents contamination by unwanted microorganisms
Names a second aseptic technique with a reason
37 °C is body temperature so harmful/pathogenic bacteria would grow; 25 °C reduces this risk

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Eukaryotic** cells have a nucleus; **prokaryotic** cells (bacteria) have a DNA loop and plasmids, and are much smaller.
- Animal cells: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes. Plant cells add a cellulose cell wall, permanent vacuole and chloroplasts.
- **Specialised cells** have features that suit one job – always link the feature to the function with *because*.
- Electron microscopes have higher **magnification and resolution** than light microscopes.
- **magnification = image size ÷ real size** – same units on top and bottom.
- Culture bacteria with **aseptic technique** and incubate at **25 °C** in school.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the substance that gives plant cell walls their strength.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell and gives it a fixed shape.

practiceQuestions.text: Which subcellular structure is the site of aerobic respiration?
practiceQuestions.hint: This structure is found in large numbers in cells that need lots of energy.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy for the cell.

options.feedback: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, not respiration.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about bacterial cells.

metadata.blanksText: Bacterial cells have no nucleus; instead their genetic material is a single loop of DNA plus small rings called ___. Their cell wall is not made of ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: The small DNA rings can carry genes for antibiotic resistance.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bacteria carry plasmids, and their cell wall is made of a different material rather than cellulose.

practiceQuestions.text: A microscope image of a bacterium is 12 mm long. The magnification is ×6000. Calculate the real length of the bacterium in micrometres.
practiceQuestions.hint: Real size = image size ÷ magnification, then convert mm to µm by multiplying by 1000.

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement best explains why an electron microscope can show ribosomes but a light microscope cannot?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the difference between magnification and resolution.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Electron microscopes have a much higher resolution, so they can distinguish very small structures such as ribosomes as separate objects.

options.text: An electron microscope has a much higher resolution.
An electron microscope uses brighter light.
options.feedback: Electron microscopes do not use light at all.

options.text: Ribosomes only exist in dead cells.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps in the correct order for transferring bacteria to an agar plate using aseptic technique.
practiceQuestions.hint: The loop must be sterile before it touches the bacteria.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sterilise the loop in the flame, let it cool briefly, dip it in the culture, streak the agar with the lid only slightly open, then tape and label the lid.
order: Pass the inoculating loop through a Bunsen flame
Dip the cooled loop into the bacterial culture
Streak the loop across the agar with the lid opened slightly
Tape the lid on and label the dish

practiceQuestions.text: Match each specialised cell to its adaptation.
practiceQuestions.hint: One cell needs to swim, one carries signals, one moves water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sperm cells use a tail to swim; nerve cells are long to carry signals over distance; xylem cells are hollow tubes for water transport.

pairs.right: Hollow tube with no end walls

practiceQuestions.text: A single bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. Calculate how many bacteria there will be after 2 hours.
practiceQuestions.hint: Work out how many divisions happen in 2 hours, then use 2 to the power of that number.

practiceQuestions.text: Muscle cells contain many more mitochondria than skin cells. Explain why.
practiceQuestions.hint: What do mitochondria do, and what do muscle cells need a lot of?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy. Muscle cells contract, which needs a lot of energy, so they need many mitochondria.

markScheme.criterion: Mitochondria carry out respiration / release energy
Muscle cells need a lot of energy to contract / move

practiceQuestions.text:
A student compares an animal cell and a plant cell under a light microscope.

(a) Give **two** structures found in the plant cell that are not found in the animal cell.

(b) The student cannot see ribosomes in either cell. Explain why.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the three extra structures plant cells have, and about what limits a light microscope.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Cell wall, chloroplasts or permanent vacuole. (b) Ribosomes are very small and a light microscope does not have a high enough resolution (or magnification) to show them.

markScheme.criterion: A second, different plant-only structure named
Light microscope lacks the resolution/magnification to show ribosomes, which are very small
